stories.text: There it is, the port of San Francisco. Fog City, Baghdad by the Bay, the Paris of the West. If you arrive there by ferry as we did, you'll be greeted by a monument not to a man of war like you would in most cities, but to a man of peace, Mahatma Gandhi, who freed India from British colonial rule without firing a shot. And if you arrive to the city By air, you may come across the sleek new terminal built in honor of another man of peace and tolerance, former city supervisor Harvey Milk, the first openly gay man to be elected to public office in California. He was assassinated by an LGBTQ hater in November 1978. It just so happens on this edition of Maui Travels, we invite you to tag along on The 52nd Annual Gay Pride Parade taking place in San Francisco. For more than 250 years, the Paris of the West, as it was once called, is one of the most diverse and tolerant cities in the world. How can you not love the Roman Gladiator in the pink and black tutu? The crowd was jubilant and people were having a blast. And you get to learn stuff too, like the contribution of the LGBTQ community over the years. Look at the marchers holding up signs of great American heroes, like computer scientist Alan Turing, astronaut Sally Rye, or botanist George Washington Carpenter. And look at the animals! You gotta love the animals, look at them! Ah, thank you! But those two in the end look a little bit like the Big Bad Wolf. The energy here was great, especially given the fact that a couple days before the Supreme Court handed down their Roe vs Wade decision, removing constitutional protection for women over their own bodies. And these guys could be next. Same-sex marriage could be next. But nothing's ever going to stop this town from partying and having a good time. And this is sad commentary on our times. stories.text: Here's the latest on little fire ants in Hawaiʻi. Originally from South America, where they had a lot of competition, little fire ants hitchhiked to Florida and then to the Big Island, likely on plants. And without their normal competitors, they multiplied to unbelievable numbers and spread to other islands. They infest plants, trees, beaches, playgrounds and yards, and create super colonies, which makes them difficult to avoid and easy to spread. The colonies are moved with potted plants, gardening supplies, yard waste, building materials and vehicles. They sting, and it hurts, leaving behind an itchy, painful rash that lasts for days or weeks. Pets and livestock Moloka are also at risk. Since they can't brush off ants or move to uninfested areas, stings to the skin and eyes can become infected and cause vision loss. The refuge was established in 1992 to provide a vital wetland home for the native and endangered Hawaiian coot Alai Keo Keo and the Hawaiian stilt, Ayo. Kuluha sedge and a kuli kuli, a sea purslane, are important native plants for the coots and stilt during their nesting season. In addition, Kaleopon is an important foraging area for migratory shorebirds and waterfowl during the winter months. Kalea Pond is the third largest remaining lowland wetland in Hawaii and the largest on Maui. So this is one of our ponds, and right now it looks like to be an important foraging pond for all of our Io that are hanging out. They just like to nest on the open mud here. They make very shallow bowls or cups. Sometimes there's vegetation included. The males and the females share incubation. You can also see we have some native plantings in here, specifically the Akuli Kuli, which is the sea purslane, that darker green, almost succulent-type looking plant. And this is a favorite for the stilts to sometimes build their nests. Hawaiian coots, or ʻAlai Kaokau, who actually is part of their diet, if they chose. So this just gives a nice diagram of our Kanoe Manu pond. Kanoe Manu means place of gathering birds. stories.text: Koki frogs are a menace. They are invasive and they are loud. Huge swaths of Hawaiʻi Island are so overrun with the dime-sized croakers that their ever-present piercing cries shatter the once-quiet tropical nights. Maui has been lucky so far. The screechers are here, but the Maui Invasive Species Committee has done a great job of keeping them in check. Now you can do something to help. Tomorrow and Wednesday at Malamahamakuā Maui in Haiku from 6 to 8 p.m. you can volunteer to spray the buggers with citrus to keep them at bay. stories.headline: Igniting Change: why Maui brushfires start and how to prepare
stories.summary: Experts say about 95 percent of Hawaiʻi wildfires are human-caused, that fallow cane and pineapple fields and climate change raise fire risk, and that homeowners should prepare evacuation plans and clear space around homes.
stories.text: The wildfires are from human causes. We've definitely seen an increase in the amount of wildfires that are occurring every year. Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization assists all the departments statewide with a lot of their statistics and tracking and I believe it's upward of 95 percent of the wildfires are caused by human sources. Now whether that's intentional or inadvertent, I've seen a lot from man-made things such as electrical lines, campfires, cars. Any of those things can They contribute to wildfires and their ignitions. So Hawaiʻi in general is pretty different in that all our wildfires primarily are started by humans. When HC&S went out of business and all those cane fields and even Maui pine, all those pineapple fields went fallow. That was when we got our worst years that I've seen. Now that Maipono has kind of taken over and now that a lot of their areas, especially in the Central Valley they've been focusing on, are getting planted, we're transitioning back to only getting fires in those historical areas where they used to be. Climate change is creating longer dry seasons, longer periods of drought, which essentially fuels wildfires. We're seeing more frequent wildfires and a lot more intense wildfires. Wildfires have a lot of fuel, essentially, with that dry vegetation. So when fires come through, it's also a very windy area. They can blow across the landscape very quickly and burn a lot of that vegetation. When we lose vegetation, all of the soil is exposed and during a storm event or a heavy rain event, all of that sediment washes down straight into Ma'alai'a Bay causing a brown water event. When we have sediment in the bay, it reduces sunlight, which is really important for photosynthesis for corals and can really stress out the coral reefs that we have here in Ma'alai'a Bay. So we work up in the mountain to establish fire breaks and plant vetiver grasses to kind of hold on to some of that soil in order to reduce potential sediment runoff. One of the biggest things a community can do from a public standpoint is preparation. There's just always being prepared that comes down to emergency evacuation plans that you have in place at your own home, Just in case these things happen so that you're safer and better prepared to get out if one of these fires comes your way. There's also getting your home better prepared. Things like having a clear space, getting fuels away from your house. They suggest up to 10 feet around your house, clearings, watching ignition sources that are in your yard, barbecues, cars that are running, any of these things that put off heat, especially during the summer months And when the conditions are right with wind and lower humidity, these all contribute to increased chances for wildfires.

stories.text: Show me the money! stories.headline: Maui Humane Society's pet of the week is Princess of Genovia
stories.summary: Princess, a dog who recovered from a fractured spine and hip, is ready for adoption, and the shelter needs kitten fosters.
stories.text: Aloha kākou. Princess of Genovia is Maui Humane Society's pet of the week. A year ago, Princess was hit by a car and came to Maui Humane Society for care. She had a fractured spine and hip. Thanks to Maui Humane Society's veterinary team and the love of her incredible foster family, She has made a beautiful recovery. Princess has been living with her foster family for almost a whole year, and they say that she is playful, potty trained, and full of personality. She adores chewy toys, sniffing for bugs, and giving kissy facials. Princess might be shy when you first meet, but she warms up quickly and will be your most loyal companion. She has come such a long way, and now she is ready to find her forever home. She is ready to be the princess of your ʻohana. Will you be her happily ever after? Your new best friend is waiting for you at Maui Himean Society, And thanks to the Bissell Pet Foundation, adoption fees are waived or reduced all month long. Dogs and cats 6 months and older plus small animals can be adopted for $0, while kittens are just $50. If you're visiting Maui, you can even arrange off-island adoptions. Help us empty the shelters. Visit mauihumainssociety.org.adopt to see our adoptable pets. Or come by the shelter today to meet your future companion. Kitten season is here. Want to help? Become a kitten foster. We are experiencing an increased influx of kittens coming into the shelter every single day and we desperately need fosters. As a foster, you will help us create critical space in our shelter for our community's sick and injured animals while you care for adorable orphan kittens at home. Maui Himei Society will provide all food, supplies, and training. You can choose to bottle feed our most fragile felines or help older kittens gain weight and learn important social skills before adoption. MHS offers training and resources for anyone interested.

stories.headline: Kyle Yamashita removed as House Finance chair
stories.summary: Fellow Democrats removed Maui Rep. Kyle Yamashita as House Finance Committee chair and replaced him with Hawaii Island Rep. Chris Todd.
stories.text: Upcountry Maui rep Kyle Yamashita is out as chair of House Finance Committee. He was shown the door by fellow Democrats yesterday after several of them expressed disappointment in Yamashita lost favor with constituents and some lawmakers by not allowing popular measures out of committee for a vote. Civil Beat reports that he was reclusive and closed himself off from the media. His office door that was often locked had a sign hung on it that said, By appointment only. stories.headline: Popular gun, marijuana and sports betting bills die in legislature
stories.summary: Bills banning assault rifles, shotguns and .50 caliber firearms, limiting magazines, and legalizing marijuana and sports wagering died in the state legislature this year.
stories.text: We reported on some of these items before, but it bears repeating for those who wish we still lived in a democracy. Some popular bills died in the state legislature this year. They include prohibitions on assault rifles, shotguns, and .50 caliber firearms. The bill, expanding bans on high-capacity detachable magazines and two favorites, recreational marijuana and wagering on sports, also bit the dust.

stories.headline: Matson container volume drops 30% amid trade war
stories.summary: Matson reported a 30% drop in April container volume, froze its workforce size, cut spending and is shifting its shipping strategy toward other parts of Ahia.
stories.text: The Trump trade war with China is taking its toll on Hawaiʻi shipping giant, Matson. The Ocean Cargo Carrier reported a 30% drop in container volume for the month of April compared to last year, and Madsen stock is sinking as well. The company has frozen the size of its workforce and has cut spending to see if it can withstand what some predict is a coming economic storm. Madsen is also adjusting shipping strategy to follow customers who have moved manufacturing to other parts of Ahia, including Vietnam.

stories.summary: The Maui Charity Walk, Hawaii's largest single-day nonprofit fundraiser, takes place Saturday from the War Memorial Complex, so drivers should watch for pedestrians.

stories.summary: The Los Angeles Rams will hold a minicamp on Maui from June 16 to 19, with a presale for Maui County residents starting May 9.
stories.text: There will be a mini camp to Maui from June 16 through the 19th and will host on-field team activities on June 17 and 18, featuring players in workout gear at War Memorial Stadium in Wailuku. The Maui camp, powered by the Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority, is being offered under a partnership to promote tourism to Maui and Hawaiʻi. stories.headline: UH Maui College sets commencement for May 15
stories.summary: UH Maui College will hold its 2025 commencement at 5:30 p.m. on Thursday, May 15, on the Great Lawn.
stories.text: Get out the caps and gowns. No more pencils, no more books, no more teachers' dirty looks, because graduation day is on its way. UH Maui College has scheduled its 2025 Commencement Ceremony for 5.30 p.m. on Thursday, May 15th, on the Great Lawn.

stories.headline: Immersion students raise funds for Washington, D.C. showcase
stories.summary: Three Hawaiian language immersion students launched a GoFundMe to raise $12,000 to present their Maunakea project at the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C.
stories.text: Three Hawaiian language immersion students, Pristine Pullman, Chukashali Smith, and A’hari Gonzalez, have launched a GoFundMe campaign looking for donations to help cover the costs of attending a 2025 ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi showcase in Washington, D.C. in June. They will collectively need to raise $12,000. The student's project explores the sacredness of Mauna Kea, and they will present it at the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian during National History Week. The event attracts nearly 3,000 students and educators from around the country.

stories.headline: Working dogs from same litter reunite after Instagram find
stories.summary: A doctor's daughter spotted Maple on Instagram and identified him as the littermate of Queens Medical Center comfort dog Mikey, leading to a reunion.
stories.text: Seeing double helped two working dogs from the same Hawaiʻi litter meet up again from across the Pacific Ocean. A doctor's daughter was scrolling on Instagram and noticed a dog that looked just like Mikey, a comfort dog at Queens Medical Center. She put on her Sherlock Holmes hat and found out that the other dog was from the same litter. The owners of the Another dog, Maple, flew in from Washington State for the four-year reunion. It turns out that, like his brother Mikey, Maple is a working dog also and serves as a guide dog for his visually impaired companion. Pretty amazing creatures, dogs.

stories.headline: Maui Travels: cruise sea day activities, part two
stories.summary: Austin Hutto and his wife show their full sea day aboard the Navigator of the Seas on a cruise to Mexico, including food, activities, shows and parties.
stories.text: Welcome back to Maui Travels. Gianna and I are cruising to Mexico. Good morning. It's day two. stories.summary: A federal judge in New York blocked a Trump order to cut over a billion dollars in unspent COVID school aid from Hawaii and 14 other states.
stories.text: A federal judge in New York today blocked a Trump order to cut more than a billion dollars in unspent COVID school aid from Hawaiʻi and 14 other states. stories.text: Medicaid is also rumored to be on the chopping block, and Medicaid cuts would be devastating to people in Hawaiʻi and 80 million people nationwide who cannot afford health care or have no health insurance. stories.headline: Insurance commissioner urges hurricane coverage check before June 1
stories.summary: Commissioner Jerry Bump warns that standard homeowners and renters policies typically don't cover hurricane and flood damage, which must be bought separately.

stories.headline: Hawaiʻi still allows child marriage

stories.text: While courts try to figure out the politics, Kīhei Charter School kids are inventing a rocket engine that could power a spacecraft to Mars and studying how sound pollution affects the call of a minor bird. stories.headline: Axis deer incentive program and overgrazing report

stories.text: Access deer are overgrazing the land in Maui County. The concept of balance is critical, especially in island ecosystems. When the carrying capacity is exceeded, environmental degradation begins, such as erosion and changes in the water cycle and plant community. Over the last several years, there has been evidence that the carrying capacity of rangelands in Maui County is being exceeded, in particular with regard to access deer, which roam freely on all three islands in the county. It is important that everyone on Maui, Molokaʻi, and Lānaʻi understands this situation. These islands are home to us all, and the condition of the land affects not only us, but future generations. Lands that are overgrazed can push damage to a tipping point of irreversible ecological damage. There is a limit to how many animals our lands can carry and still be healthy. To help illustrate what is happening, let us walk through a scenario based on some assumptions about In this example, one of these equals a thousand deer. In early 2022, a survey was done that found about 46,000 deer on part of Maui. Let's assume the deer population on Maui is 50,000 deer. Based on herd observations, it is estimated the herd is mostly female. So let's assume that 80% or 40,000 deer are female. Axis deer are known to be prolific producers. We will We assume 90% of all the female deer give birth to one fawn each year, so that the herd would grow by 36,000 deer each year. According to reports, roughly 16,000 deer were hunted or harvested in 2022. Since this harvest rate is less than the estimated reproductive rate, we can logically conclude the herd will continue to grow. After one year, the herd is now up to 70,000, with more females reproducing and the herd growing again. If the numbers were If we get too high at 50,000 causing overgrazing that was hurting the environment, the damage will get even worse every year unless we turn this around and start moving toward balancing the system. We can't make more land, we can't make it rain, the number of animals needs to be managed. Continued overgrazing by excessive wildlife populations will cause further degradation of land and near shore waters in Maui County. This chart shows the projected exponential We need to increase the growth rate of deer population in Maui County if we don't figure out how to effectively manage the population. If this happens, we can expect increasing conflict with people as deer get desperate and move into farms, residential, commercial and resort areas, and along roads. Bare ground will increase and with that, soil erosion will increase, increasing flooding and affecting the quality of our air and water as soil blows and washes away. And when we lose too much soil, the land eventually cannot support vegetation. Without vegetation, the land cannot absorb water to help with recharging our aquifers. Bare ground is also hot, exacerbating drought effects for plants, animals, and people. Overgrazing can lead to eventual ecological collapse. This is just an example of how prolific the population growth of Axis deer is, and how significant the effort needs to be to manage the deer and keep their numbers at sustainable levels. The Axis deer are native to Southeast Ahia, Where there are at least nine natural predators that keep their population in check. Here in Maui County, there's only one, people. This is a big problem affecting our island. We need to work together in a coordinated effort to find solutions for the health of our land, our animals, our community, our future generations. Cute, but really harmful to the environment.

stories.headline: Hoʻokipa Maui Marketplace returns May 29
stories.summary: The tradeshow-style Hoʻokipa Maui Marketplace returns May 29 at the Sheraton Maui Resort & Spa after a 2024 debut with more than 80 local businesses.
stories.text: Hoʻokipa is not just a famous windsurfing spot. stories.summary: A husband-and-wife team bakes family recipes like empanadas and sourdough at Pau Bakery in Lahaina.

stories.headline: Free Mokuʻula 360 film screens Friday at The Sphere
stories.summary: A free 360-degree animated film about Mokuʻula screens Friday, May 9 at 6 p.m. at Maui Ocean Center's The Sphere, with reservations required.

stories.headline: Free legal advice by phone during Law Week
stories.summary: Volunteer attorneys give free legal advice by phone from 6 to 7 p.m. each evening through Saturday at 808 537-1868.

stories.headline: Love the Sea volunteers clean up Maui beaches
stories.summary: Campbell Ferrell of Love the Sea describes cleanups that netted industrial fishing gear and plastics, and the group's plans for more hard-to-reach beach cleanups.

stories.headline: Four hurt in head-on crash on Hana Highway
stories.summary: Four people were taken to the hospital with major injuries after a GMC Sierra truck collided with a Nissan Altima on Hana Highway Friday afternoon, and speed is thought to be a factor.
stories.text: Four people were involved in a head-on collision on Hana Highway at Spreckelsville Friday afternoon at 3.43 p.m. A GMC Sierra truck attempting to pass other cars collided with a Nissan Altima. stories.headline: State Senate confirms eight family and circuit court judges

stories.headline: MIL surfing championship held in Lahaina Harbor

stories.headline: $10 million backs zero-down loans for Native Hawaiians
stories.summary: Northern Trust and Hawaiʻi Community Lending announced a $10 million investment in the Kūpaʻa Hale Loan program offering zero-down mortgages to Native Hawaiians on Hawaiian Home Lands.

stories.headline: Letter carriers to collect food for Stamp Out Hunger
stories.summary: On Saturday, residents can leave non-perishable food by their mailboxes for postal carriers to collect for the Maui Food Bank.
stories.text: Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds. stories.headline: Legislature raises hotel tax to 11 percent
stories.summary: The legislature raised the Transient Accomodation Tax from 10.25% to 11%, and counties added 3% more, for an expected combined $100 million a year.

stories.headline: Major bills failed at the legislature as some taxes rose
stories.summary: Bills that failed include a wealth tax, vacant home tax and online gambling, while lawmakers raised taxes on cigarettes, increased vehicle registration fees and phased out income tax credits.
stories.text: A number of major bills failed at the sausage factory, otherwise known as our state legislature. Bills that didn't make the cut include a wealth tax, vacant home tax, exempting groceries from general excise tax, online gambling, film industry credits, and a bill that would increase penalties for bribery.
